rent-calculator.quickAnswer: The 30% rule says rent should not exceed 30% of gross income: max rent = annual income x 0.30 / 12. Example: on 1,200,000 annual income you can afford up to 30,000 per month, with a conservative 25,000 target at the 25% rule. If your current 25,000 rent is 25% of your monthly income, you are in the comfortable zone.
keyFacts: The 30% rule: spend no more than 30% of gross income on rent.
The 25% rule is the conservative version that leaves more room for savings.
Landlords often use the 40x rule: annual income should be 40x the monthly rent (same math as 30%).
Rent burden above 30% is called cost-burdened; above 50% is severely burdened.
These rules use gross income; your take-home budget is tighter.
High-cost cities force many renters above 30%: then cut other costs or earn more, not wishful math.
howTo: Optionally enter your current or quoted monthly rent.
Read your maximum affordable rent under the 30% rule.
Use the 25% figure as your comfort target when house-hunting.
Check the verdict: it grades your current rent against your income.
rent-calculator.formula:
Max monthly rent (30% rule) = Annual income x 0.30 / 12.
Conservative rent (25% rule) = Annual income x 0.25 / 12.
Rent burden = (Monthly rent / Monthly income) x 100.
Example: 1,200,000 x 0.30 / 12 = 30,000; burden of 25,000 rent = 25%.
rent-calculator.workedExample:
Annual income 1,200,000, current rent 25,000:
1. Max rent: 1,200,000 x 0.30 / 12 = 30,000 per month.
2. Conservative target: 1,200,000 x 0.25 / 12 = 25,000 per month.
3. Monthly income: 1,200,000 / 12 = 100,000.
4. Rent burden: 25,000 / 100,000 x 100 = 25%.
5. Verdict: 25% is at or under 30%, so this rent is affordable with room to save.
benefits: Stops you from falling in love with a flat your budget cannot keep.
Gives landlords' own 40x rule back to you as a negotiating fact.
The conservative target protects your savings rate while renting.
The burden verdict grades any listing against your income in one glance.
limitations: Rules of thumb, not personal finance advice: your debts and goals matter too.
Uses gross income; taxes and deductions shrink what is truly available.
Ignores utilities, maintenance, and commuting costs that add to housing cost.
In very high or low cost cities the 30% rule fits poorly; adjust with judgment.

faqs.a: It is the long-standing housing affordability standard used by governments and lenders: at 30% most households can still cover food, transport, savings, and debt. It is a ceiling, not a target; spending less is always better.
Landlords often require annual income of 40 times the monthly rent. It is the same math as the 30% rule: 12 / 0.30 = 40. If a landlord quotes it, you now know exactly where the number comes from.

faqs.q: Should I use gross or net income?
faqs.a: These rules are defined on gross income, so enter gross for the standard answer. For your real budget, repeat the math on take-home pay: that number is the one your bank account feels.

faqs.q: My rent is 40% of my income. What now?
faqs.a: First, verify with net income, since gross flatters the ratio. Then either raise income, find a cheaper place or roommates, or cut other spending deliberately. Do not just hope it works out: a 40% burden leaves almost no margin for emergencies.

faqs.q: Does this include utilities and maintenance?
faqs.a: No. The 30% rule covers rent alone in its classic form. Add your expected utilities, society charges, and commuting cost to the rent before judging affordability honestly.

faqs.q: Is renting at 25% always better than 30%?
faqs.a: For your savings rate, yes: that 5% difference compounds into real wealth over the years. But do not pick a terrible location just to hit 25%; commute time and safety have value too.

labels.burdenOk: At or under 30%: this rent is affordable with room to save.
labels.burdenHigh: Between 30% and 40%: tight, consider cheaper options or higher income.
labels.burdenSevere: Above 40%: severely burdened, this rent strains your budget.
